1. The Velari tunnel — fixed rules
Built by the Velari, not by humans. Its age is unknown and probably measured in millennia.

Pilot throat: permanently open and submicroscopic. It accepts only a fixed, extremely low-bandwidth synchronization and mathematical-challenge vocabulary; it cannot carry addressable audio, telemetry, or mission data.
Activation occurs when a civilization demonstrates the ability to detect and interpret it and consciously accepts. The challenge is a passive filter; the opening cannot be triggered accidentally.
Expansion to navigable diameter demands extreme energy that scales nonlinearly. Even the Velari can sustain it for only 60–90 seconds and cannot reopen it immediately at will.
Crossing stages: preload (cancelable) → critical expansion (commit point; unsafe to cancel) → navigable opening (60–90 s) → collapse.

The local mouth occupies a controlled halo orbit around Sol–Jupiter L2 under active Velari stabilization. The remote mouth is fixed infrastructure in its own orbit near the meeting region and cannot be moved without expansion-scale energy.

There is no ring. Each mouth is a field of black nodes separated by kilometres or tens of kilometres. During expansion, distortions and filaments connect them; the final navigable region is about 150–200 m wide.
2. Proxima — origin and operation

Original purpose: Jovian observatory and gravitational laboratory, built before Velari technology was recognized. The story extrapolates from fictional navigation residuals in Pioneer, Voyager, Galileo, and Juno data; it does not claim a real discovery.

A network of drag-free probes, optical clocks, laser interferometry, and test masses locates the pilot throat at L2. Xenophysics, communications, contact control, and mission support are added only afterward.

Architecture: a 500–800 m non-rotating spine with axial docks, tanks, workshops, control, reactors, and antennas; two counter-rotating cylindrical habitats at 0.4–0.6 g; perpendicular radiators and storage; hazardous modules isolated on arms.
Normal power comes from fusion, with independent fission for critical loads and Jovian deuterium/helium-3 logistics.
Life support recycles more than 95% of its water, regenerates oxygen, removes CO₂, and holds months of reserves. Water, polymers, and consumables contribute to shielding.
Different construction generations must remain visible: an aged scientific core, industrial additions, and a recent contact layer—not a station built all at once for the Velari.

blocks: Before crossing, the radiators retract, the torch shuts down, and heat moves into accumulators. They deploy again before the next burn. Apparent gravity does not reverse during turnover: it vanishes in free fall and returns toward the same deck after rotation.
Interior: decks transverse to thrust, three axial cylinders—central, service, and logistics—and an off-axis retrofit diplomatic core.
Bridge: the axial vestibule and central exit sit behind the crew in Voss’s frontal composition; the service access is recessed beyond the consoles’ sightline.
Engine-off circulation: bars and rests in the central cylinder; fast ballistic travel among trays and branches in the service cylinder.
Communications: wireless mesh plus wired COM A/B on every deck. A distributor near command gathers sector-labelled couplers.
External laser: standard long-range equipment with local control and aiming on a dedicated physical route.
4. Velari architecture — canonical observations

Velari station: a continuous organic habitat several kilometres across, without visible assembled modules. Lobes, arches, cavities, voids, and a skin able to change reflectivity, texture, transparency, geometry, and emissivity.
The entire skin can radiate in infrared. No separate reactor, fuel, tanks, or exhaust can be identified—only immense energy gradients.

It does not spin and generates controlled local gravity. Human sensors find life-compatible temperatures, circulating liquids, complex chemistry, and pressurized zones: more built ecosystem than mechanical station.

Emissary ship: 300–600 m, organic and bioluminescent; huge beside Celestial Ardor and small beside the station. No nozzles or exhaust; metric disturbances imply momentum exchange with external structures or fields.
Its reconfigurable interior is an instrumental inference or feature-length material, not information the humans must explain in the short.

6. Launch window — two independent, ranked constraints
Hard constraint: Sol–Jupiter–remote-anchor geometry (~11.86 years), which determines when a macroscopic throat can stabilize and roughly matches Jupiter’s orbital period.
Secondary constraint: stored energy, which limits the opening to 60–90 seconds. Energy may be ready sooner but cannot replace the required geometry.
Orbital separation after 12 years (remote mouth versus Velari station, currently near a node between differently inclined orbits):

Canonical configuration: ~30° inclination. Current mission separation is ~0.122 AU (18.3×10⁶ km); in 12 years it is about 24 times greater. A comparable orbital crossing may take more than a thousand years, with no guarantee of an exact match if period or eccentricity also differ.
Conclusion: the current window is very likely unique on a human-lifetime scale.
7. Zao’s message
Final content: ‘If this arrives… Acheron is inside. Harlan altered the core. The surface log is false. Cross-check the routine against the physical relay. Don’t shut down mediation. Please…’
First warning: the bridge hears that an autonomous payload bears Sorell’s signature and that the signature appears false. The cutoff prevents them from hearing Harlan’s name.
Block: Harlan activates a jammer at the bridge access and disconnects DIPLOMATIC SYSTEMS — COM A/B in the service-cylinder distributor. Wireless, text, and both wired backups fail.
Available path: the external laser is the standard long-range system; local control retains power and command through dedicated physical routing.
Aim: Zao combines the flight plan, light time, and the ship’s future position. Beam divergence covers part of the uncertainty ellipse and a narrow sweep covers the rest.
Rejected destinations: Earth would deliver the warning after the encounter; Proxima has no useful optical acquisition; the pilot throat cannot carry mission data.
Harlan cannot stop reception because the pointing solution is already closed. He sees TRANSMITTED but not the exact corridor.
Signal travel time: ~23 h 15 min (167.8 AU).
Causal double key

Investigation without message: Elin identifies the autonomous payload, trigger, and required quarantine, but obtains only anonymous signature OVR-7C41. She cannot prove who owns the override or stop that owner from releasing it.
Message without investigation: it accuses Harlan and names the relay, but cannot prove the voice is genuine or supply the technical map needed to stop a process that remains active after arrest.
Together: payload, physical relay, and command credential identify Harlan; Voss revokes his authority and Elin applies her prepared quarantine. Sorell supplies the clean passive greeting.
8. Harlan’s motive / Acheron Directive — canonical text

The Acheron Directive does not seek war as an end; it accepts war as a calculated risk. It holds that offering humanity’s diplomatic credentials without verification to a civilization millennia more advanced could cost the species. Harlan prefers verifiable intelligence about Velari defenses—even if obtaining it reads as aggression—to blind surrender. This is not technological greed but preventive self-defense applied by someone convinced he alone sees clearly.

Acheron is a public, decentralized doctrine rather than a membership organization. Its protests are legal and visible; the sabotage cell is clandestine. Harlan passed screening because there was no verifiable affiliation to declare or detect.

The sabotage was not rushed: he had 57 h 48 min to execute it carefully. The physical record is unavoidable—every emergency override burns an anonymous signature into hardware, and erasing it would disable the core. He accepts that risk, trusting the surface forgery, Zao’s death, and his authority to keep the pieces apart.

blocks: 11. Consolidation decisions in this pass

Jupiter occultation and automatic crossing partition are no longer the central mechanisms. Harlan isolates Zao with a jammer and physical COM A/B cut, then uses the service cylinder in microgravity to beat Sorell to her station. An Earth relay remains too slow.
Rounding differences in signal time were resolved in favor of the independently verified ~23 h 15 min figure; the difference has no dramatic effect.
Thirty minutes is an editing target, not a proven duration. A timed read and actual animatic must validate it.

Immediate availability is not coincidence: Proxima, Ardor, and her crew already served Jovian operations; the diplomatic core was installed during years of study, and the 60-hour warning requires only final preparation and boarding.

Visible technology expresses different levels: human systems expose tanks, radiators, joints, and redundancy; Velari systems hide the boundaries between structure, propulsion, life support, and heat rejection.

CHARACTERS (short-film cast)

ZAO — Chief Engineer. She uncovers the sabotage during transit, sends the emergency message, and is murdered minutes before the crossing. She is the story’s emotional engine. In her forties or fifties, practical build, dark gray or navy engineering coveralls, tools at her belt. She informally mentors Elin and trusts Sorell’s linguistic work.
CAPTAIN ELIAS VOSS — Ship commander. He must preserve order on a journey with no return and no consultation with Earth. In his fifties, upright, graying.

COMMANDER RYLEN HARLAN — Saboteur and career officer, secretly aligned with an operational Acheron cell. He acts from preventive-defense conviction, not greed. His emergency single-officer override opens maintenance mode and burns an anonymous, indelible signature into the physical relay; command can revoke it once its owner is identified.

ELIN RAO — AI specialist. She discovers the payload’s autonomous behavior, extracts its technical signature, and prepares the quarantine that stops it without destroying mediation. Zao involves her from launch and teaches her to isolate advanced corruption instead of repairing it. Elin works from a protected bridge terminal; investigation and message are both required.

DR. LIAN SORELL — Xenolinguist. Harlan’s planted surface evidence temporarily sidelines her. Once cleared, she shows the payload is not Velari language and supplies the clean, read-only greeting prepared before launch.

LT. JUNO CAEL — Pilot / Communications. Pragmatic bridge voice; pilots the 57 h 48 min local transit and 24-hour remote leg, then detects and authenticates Zao’s incoming signal. She remotely forces the core closed without leaving navigation.
On-screen supporting characters
PROXIMA TECHNICIAN — dock maintenance and control staff. Graphite workwear with ochre accents distinguishes station crew from the mission’s navy uniforms.
CELESTIAL ARDOR MEDICAL OFFICER — examines Zao and establishes that her injuries are not a fall. Petrol-blue flight medical uniform, without a modern hospital coat.
SECURITY CREWMEMBER — attempts to restrain Harlan and accompanies Voss into the core. Charcoal uniform with flexible protection and restraints; no firearms.

EARTH PROTESTERS — two currents shown with equal seriousness in news footage: Acheron fear and preventive defense versus cautious hope for contact. Palette, geometry, and behavior distinguish them without moral caricature.
Characters reserved for a longer version
Okoye, Volkov, Keene, Vega, Carvalho, Tanaka, Hassan, and Wei do not appear in the current short. Their functions, ages, and relationships must be defined before their visual design is fixed.
LOCATIONS

PROXIMA STATION — controlled halo orbit around Sol–Jupiter L1. A pre-contact Jovian science station with an old observational core and later shipyard, storage, xenophysics, communications, and contact-control additions. A 500–800 m non-rotating spine, counter-rotating habitats, axial docks, black radiators, and isolated hazardous arms read as ISS + refinery + shipyard.

THE MOUTH — controlled halo orbit around Sol–Jupiter L2. Not a ring: black nodes spread across kilometres surround a nearly undetectable void. Critical expansion produces filaments, impossible lensing, and unfamiliar light; a 150–200 m navigable region exists for only 60–90 seconds.

CELESTIAL ARDOR — INTERIOR. Transverse decks and three longitudinal routes: everyday central cylinder, lift shaft, and narrow service cylinder for ballistic travel and technical trays. The bridge opens to a visible axial vestibule while service access hides in a side recess. The off-axis retrofit diplomatic core has separate operational and technical access; a nearby distributor gathers deck COM A/B couplers. Thrust gives 1 g; final approach and crossing are in microgravity.
REMOTE MOUTH — functional twin of the local mouth, fixed near the meeting region and movable only at expansion-scale cost.

MEETING REGION / VELARI STATION — about 18.3 million km from the remote mouth. A continuous, kilometre-scale organic habitat with lobes, arches, cavities, bioluminescent adaptive skin, controlled local gravity, pressurized zones, and circulating liquids. An emissary craft departs it for the rendezvous.
EARTH — appears only in opening news screens: demonstrations for and against contact.
SHIPS

CELESTIAL ARDOR — 80–100 m, ~300 t, long-duration Earth ship retrofitted for diplomacy. Matte white/silver hull, gold details, long axial form, magnetic nozzle, liquid-metal radiators, D–³He torch, 70–80 t of fuel and reaction mass, and two-week endurance for six.

VELARI EMISSARY — 300–600 m, organic, curved, and bioluminescent. No nozzles or exhaust; metric disturbances imply propulsion coupled to the environment. Its interior appears reconfigurable for different biologies.
PROPS
QUANTUM DIPLOMATIC CORE — pulsing sphere/crystal: blue when nominal, red when corrupted. It also houses the mediation AI; these are one system, not two.

EXTERNAL COMMUNICATIONS LASER — Ardor’s standard long-range system. Local control, power, and aiming use a dedicated physical route separate from wireless and COM A/B. Zao aims it at the ship’s future corridor using the flight plan, light time, divergence, and a narrow sweep. It signs device and time, not the truth of the message.

PHYSICAL RELAY RECORD — anonymous hardware trace burned by every override and impossible to alter without disabling the core. It differs from the falsifiable surface log implicating Sorell and becomes conclusive only when combined with Elin’s isolated routine and Zao’s message.
SORELL’S GREETING PACKAGE — passive, non-executable, read-only sequence stored before launch. Elin can transmit it over a clean channel after isolating the payload.
THROAT / EXPANSION INDICATOR — PRELOAD → CRITICAL EXPANSION → NAVIGABLE OPENING (60–90 s countdown) → COLLAPSE. It replaces the obsolete ‘occlusion’ indicator.
NEWS SCREENS — Proxima dock displays the Earth protest/celebration montage with a visible Earth-to-station signal-delay indicator.

I. General concept

Light Delay is a hard-science-fiction thriller centered on the final message of an engineer murdered aboard humanity’s first-contact mission to the ancient Velari. Real constraints of light propagation and orbital mechanics combine with alien—not human—interstellar transit technology to shape plot and tension.

The mission does not depart at a time chosen for human convenience. Millennia-old Velari infrastructure activates for the first time, opening a transit window that may not recur for more than a thousand years.
II. Mission context
The Velari Gate

Near Sol–Jupiter L2 lies a Velari pilot throat: permanently open but submicroscopic. It carries only fixed synchronization and mathematical-challenge pulses, not general audio, telemetry, or mission data.

Detection precedes contact. Fictional residuals in Pioneer, Voyager, Galileo, and Juno navigation motivate a dedicated network. Proxima is built at L1 as a Jovian science station and gravitational laboratory; drag-free probes, optical clocks, interferometry, and test masses eventually locate the artificial anomaly near L2.

The discovery transforms existing infrastructure. Proxima adds xenophysics and contact systems; the already-stationed Celestial Ardor receives a diplomatic core. Elin and Zao help interpret the protocol, and conscious human authorization starts a 60-hour countdown to a 60–90-second navigable opening.

Macroscopic expansion demands extreme, nonlinear energy. Stored energy sets duration; Sol–Jupiter–remote-anchor geometry sets when it can stabilize. The next comparable local phase is about 11.86 years later.

The Velari station also moves relative to the fixed remote mouth. They are now near an orbital node but still 0.122 AU apart; in 12 years separation may approach 3 AU, and the next comparable node may take over a millennium. This is probably humanity’s only contact opportunity for generations.
Reaction on Earth

The opening divides public opinion. Optimists celebrate; the decentralized Acheron Directive demands suspension because the Velari control the gate. It has no formal membership list, while a clandestine operational cell includes Harlan.
Sixty hours leave no time for public debate. Ardor already operates from Proxima and needs only final preparation, contact specialists, and equipment.
The ship

Celestial Ardor is an Earth-built long-duration exploration and science vessel retrofitted for diplomacy: 80–100 m, ~300 t, axial, with forward sensors, central bridge/habitat/shelter, retrofit diplomatic core, and aft tanks, reactor, and fusion torch. Wear, joints, locks, and service lines keep it visibly maintained rather than pristine.

A D–³He torch and magnetic nozzle support 1 g / 1 g flight. Some 70–80 t of fuel and reaction mass cover both legs and limited contingencies. Liquid-metal radiators retract for crossing; an auxiliary reactor sustains critical loads. Endurance is about two weeks for six.
Proxima Station

Proxima occupies a controlled halo orbit around L1. Its 500–800 m non-rotating spine holds axial docks, lifts, control, workshops, storage, antennas, and reactors; counter-rotating habitats provide 0.4–0.6 g, with radiators and hazardous modules extending outward.
Its silhouette reads observatory + refinery + shipyard. Old truss, laboratories from different eras, and recent xenotechnology explain decades of study and a mission prepared in sixty hours.
III. The journey — transit mechanics
Local leg: Proxima (L1) → tunnel mouth (L2)

Ardor crosses ~106 million km on a powered arc around Jupiter, accelerating at 1 g for half the trip and braking at 1 g for the rest. It neither crosses Jupiter nor relies on a major gravity assist. Total transit is 57 h 48 min, peaking near 1,020 km/s.

The drive supports about 90 accumulated hours at 1 g. Turnover occurs in free fall and apparent gravity returns toward the same deck. An unlimited ideal system could cross 167.8 AU in ~37 days at ~15,700 km/s, but Ardor lacks the reaction mass, endurance, and heat rejection; the tunnel is essential.
The crossing

The mouth is not a ring. Black nodes spread over kilometres surround empty space, then non-Euclidean distortions connect them through preload, critical expansion, a 60–90-second navigable opening, and collapse. Only then does a 150–200 m passage appear.
The crossing is virtually instantaneous from the ship’s perspective.
Remote leg: remote mouth → Velari station

On the far side, Ardor redeploys radiators and flies another 24-hour 1 g / 1 g profile over 18.3 million km. The station is a multi-kilometre organic habitat with local gravity, adaptive radiating skin, circulating liquids, and pressurized zones but no separable reactor, fuel, or life-support system.

A 300–600 m Velari emissary leaves the station for the first direct meeting. It has no visible engines or exhaust and appears reconfigurable for different biologies, preserving the station as destination and the emissary as the finale’s dramatic presence.
IV. Zao’s discovery and death
Zao’s isolation

Zao is correctly stationed at the diplomatic core. Harlan reaches the bridge entrance unseen as she reports an autonomous payload signed by Sorell and says the signature appears false. Before she can name him, he remotely activates a jammer and slips toward the service cylinder.

Across the 57 h 48 min transit, Zao gathers power anomalies, an off-hours access, and code hidden in linguistic protocol. By T+40 h she can prove only a dangerous wrapper and works with Elin without accusing Sorell. Critical expansion reveals an autonomous intrusion scan and an indelible but anonymous hardware signature.

The jammer kills voice, text, and wireless. Harlan disconnects DIPLOMATIC SYSTEMS — COM A/B from the service distributor before Zao can use wired backup, then travels ballistically through the service tube. Sorell moves more slowly along handrails. The only surviving path is local control of Ardor’s standard external laser on dedicated physical routing.
Why she does not transmit toward Earth
Even without blocking, an Earth relay adds enough light time for the warning to arrive after the Velari encounter. Only a direct beam toward the crew’s future position can still help.
The message

The loaded flight plan already tells Zao where the ship must be after crossing. Under pressure she solves the pointing geometry, sets divergence and a narrow sweep for the uncertainty corridor, and transmits. The signal travels ~23 h 15 min. Device and time signatures prove only that it left her console, not that its accusation is true.
She transmits:
‘If this arrives… Acheron is inside. Harlan altered the core. The surface log is false. Cross-check the routine against the physical relay. Don’t shut down mediation. Please…’

Message and investigation form a double key. Elin knows what the payload does and how to contain it but cannot identify the override owner; Zao names Harlan and the relay but supplies neither proof nor the neutralization method. Together they let Voss revoke Harlan and Elin quarantine the attack without disabling mediation.

Harlan arrives after the pointing solution closes, sees TRANSMITTED but not the corridor, kills Zao, cleans his traces, and returns by the service cylinder. Sorell arrives later, attempts resuscitation, and cannot reach the bridge while the jammer remains active. Harlan returns to command and claims not to have seen her. The ship crosses with no way to abort or return.
V. Harlan’s motive

Harlan does not seek war. He believes handing humanity’s technological credentials to a far older civilization without verification could cost the species. He prefers defensible intelligence—even acquired by a method the Velari may read as aggression—to blind surrender. His doctrine is preventive self-defense, not greed.

The altered diplomatic core hides autonomous scanning and intrusion inside a peaceful exchange. It would penetrate Velari systems and send Earth a biased record of the response. Harlan accepts the ship’s likely loss so destruction, expulsion, or permanent closure can later be framed as unprovoked hostility.
VI. Plot structure
ACT I — Transit and throat. Sixty-hour activation; final preparation; 57 h 48 min of growing clues; discovery, emergency transmission, murder, and crossing.

ACT II — Investigation in strange space. The body, medical review, missing cameras, planted evidence against Sorell, Elin’s autonomous-payload discovery and incomplete anonymous signature, Harlan’s pressure to disable mediation, and detection of a weak incoming signal.

ACT III — Signal and survival. Zao’s message arrives 40–45 minutes before contact; evidence converges; Harlan triggers early; his override is revoked; Elin quarantines the sabotage; Sorell’s clean greeting is sent; the Velari authorize approach.

VIII. Themes and symbolism
Light delay as metaphor: truth arrives too late to prevent tragedy, just in time to alter the outcome.
A gate humanity neither built nor fully understands: vulnerability as a condition of genuine first contact.
Reasonable fear and radicalization: Harlan is the extreme wing of a legitimate, widely shared doubt.
Heroism without witnesses: Zao’s actions remain unseen until the light literally catches up.
IX. Tone and genre
Tense, cerebral, claustrophobic: hard science fiction, mystery, and political thriller. Tonal references include The Expanse, Arrival, 2001: A Space Odyssey, and Tenet.
